title: Steps to the Nearest Exit
statement:
A floor plan is a grid rooms. Each cell holds one of three values: -1 is a wall, 0 is an exit, and 2147483647 (call it FAR) is an open room. You can step between cells that share a side, but never into a wall.

Change the grid in place: replace every open room with the number of steps from it to the nearest exit. A room that cannot reach any exit keeps the value FAR. Walls and exits stay as they are. Return nothing.

examples.why: Each room takes its nearest exit. The room at (1, 1) is 3 steps from the bottom exit but 2 from the top one, so it gets 2. The room at (0, 0) is closer to the bottom exit, even though it shares a row with the top one.
The wall cuts the room off from the only exit, so it keeps FAR.
The room at index 3 is 2 steps from the first exit but 1 from the second. Filling from the first exit alone would give 2.

hints: Running a search from every room is slow. Is there a direction that needs fewer searches?
Search from the exits instead. But one search per exit still repeats work when there are many exits. What if all exits started at the same time?
Put every exit into one BFS queue at distance 0. The first time BFS reaches a room is along its shortest path to the closest exit, so write the distance then and never touch that room again.

explain.intuition:
You want, for every room, the distance to the closest of several exits. Running BFS from each exit and keeping the minimum works, but with thousands of exits that is thousands of full-grid searches.

Start one BFS from all exits at once. Picture a hidden super-exit connected to every real exit with a zero-length step: BFS from it reaches each room first along the shortest route to whichever exit is nearest. Because BFS hands out distances in increasing order, the first value written into a room is final. The grid itself is the visited set: a room still holding FAR has not been reached yet.
steps: Push the position of every exit (value 0) into a queue.
Pop a cell. For each neighbour inside the grid whose value is still FAR, set it to this cell's value plus one and push it.
Walls are never FAR, so they are skipped automatically. Exits are 0, so they are never overwritten.
When the queue is empty, every reachable room holds its distance and the rest still hold FAR.
pitfalls: Running a full BFS from each exit. It is correct but costs O(exits · cells), which is far too slow when exits are common.
Starting from each room and searching for an exit. That is O(cells²) in the worst case and repeats almost the same search for neighbouring rooms.

Updating a room that already has a distance. With a single multi-source BFS the first value is the smallest; overwriting it with a later, larger value gives wrong answers like 2 instead of 1 in example 3.

solutions.title: BFS from each exit separately
solutions.idea: For every exit, run a full BFS with its own visited set and lower each room's value when this exit is closer. Correct, but the work grows with the number of exits.

solutions.title: One BFS from all exits at once
solutions.idea: Seed the queue with every exit. A room still holding FAR is unvisited; the first distance written into it is the shortest.

followups: Also record which exit each room is closest to. What extra value travels through the queue?
Some doors take 2 steps to pass through. Why does the plain BFS order break, and what would you use instead?
